title: Trump Orders Warning Signs Outside Smithsonian Over 'Inaccurate' History Exhibits
excerpt: The executive order directs the National Park Service to install signage near the National Museum of American History, escalating a culture war over how the country tells its own story.
body:
• President Trump signed an executive order directing warning signs be placed outside the Smithsonian's National Museum of American History
  • The signs will reference a 162-page White House report that accused the museum of "radical" left-wing ideological capture
  • The Smithsonian operates independently of the executive branch, but Trump is leveraging federal control of surrounding sidewalks
  • Museum Director Anthea Hartig testified this week that the report "does not fairly or accurately characterize" the museum's work

President Donald Trump signed an executive order on Friday directing the National Park Service to install temporary warning signs outside the Smithsonian's National Museum of American History, marking his most direct intervention yet in a months-long clash over how the nation's premier history museum tells America's story.

The order instructs the NPS — which controls the sidewalks outside several Smithsonian museums on the National Mall — to place signage notifying visitors that exhibits "should be renovated" in line with the findings of a White House report. The signs will also point visitors to unspecified "locations and resources for accurate information" about American history.

The White House Report

The directive stems from a 162-page report published on July 4 by the White House Domestic Policy Council, titled "Restoring Truth and Sanity to American History." The report accused the Smithsonian of advancing what it called "thinly veiled anti-Americanism" and "extreme political activism that seeks to transform our country," according to CNN.

https://x.com/FoxNews/status/2080839302146035790

"The Smithsonian Institution, and the National Museum of American History in particular, under its current leadership and current interpretive ideology, cannot be trusted to tell America's story honestly and in a way that is inspiring, unifying, and worthy of our great republic," the report stated.

"President Trump is fighting back to restore one of the Nation's greatest civic treasures to its founding mission and purpose and reestablish truth in the Nation's historical narrative."

— White House fact sheet

An Independent Institution Under Pressure

The Smithsonian is an independent agency designed to operate outside the executive branch's direct control — Trump cannot unilaterally remove museum leadership or change exhibits. Instead, the executive order targets federal property outside the museum that falls under NPS jurisdiction, according to Fox News.

But the administration holds other points of leverage. The government controls much of the Smithsonian's funding, and Vice President JD Vance sits on its board of regents. The Trump administration has also directed the creation of a temporary exhibit intended to present what it considers a corrected version of American history.

Friday's order builds on a March 2025 executive order in which the White House sought to combat what it called "historical revisions" that cast the country's history in a negative light. It also follows the appointment of administration allies to key oversight roles within the museum system.

Museum Leaders Push Back

During congressional testimony this week, National Museum of American History Director Anthea Hartig defended her institution's work. "As we continue to fact-check the report, we unwaveringly attest that it does not fairly or accurately characterize the full body of work at the museum," Hartig told lawmakers, according to Fox News.

"The museum does not take sides in America's political debates," she added. "We preserve and document the evidence of American life in all of its breadth, so that the public can encounter the past and draw their own conclusions."

Smithsonian Institution Secretary Lonnie Bunch also rejected the report's characterization of the museum's programming.

The move has drawn sharp criticism from some lawmakers. Rep. Terri Sewell (D-AL) compared the administration's scrutiny to "fascism" during a House Administration Committee hearing, according to the Washington Examiner. David Blight, a historian who testified as the Democrats' witness, likened the effort to patterns seen in "authoritarian regimes."

What It Means

The Smithsonian declined to comment on Friday's order, according to CNN. But the confrontation over one of America's most visited cultural institutions — which draws tens of millions of visitors annually — is unlikely to end with sidewalk signage. Trump has signaled that exhibit changes and leadership reviews are next, setting the stage for a prolonged battle over who gets to shape the country's official historical narrative.

For Indian Americans and other immigrant communities whose stories are woven into the museum's exhibits on migration, civil rights, and cultural contributions, the outcome could shape how their heritage is publicly represented in the nation's capital.
